outline.description: This chapter sets out the factual backdrop of the dispute, introduces the parties, describes how the alleged infringement arose through the Cameo platform, outlines the district court’s ruling, and explains the procedural posture before the Second Circuit.
subtopics: Identification of plaintiff George Santos and defendants Jimmy Kimmel, ABC/Disney
Cameo video requests: fictitious names, Santos’s fulfillment of personalized videos
Broadcast of the videos on Jimmy Kimmel Live! as part of the "Will Santos Say It?" segment
District Court’s Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal of copyright infringement claims on fair‑use grounds
Dismissal of state‑law breach‑of‑contract and fraudulent‑inducement claims
Appeal filing in the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Rule 12(b)(6) Pleading Standard and Judicial Notice in Copyright Cases
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal standards governing a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim, how appellate courts review such motions de novo, and the role of judicial notice over copyright registrations when assessing pleadings.
subtopics: The Twombly‑Iqbal plausibility standard for Rule 12(b)(6) motions
"De novo" review versus deference to district‑court factual findings
Scope of factual allegations considered at the pleading stage (citing DiFolco v. MSNBC)
Judicial notice power over publicly filed copyright registrations (Island Software v. Microsoft)
Why fair‑use analysis can be conducted on the face of a complaint

outline.chapter_title: Fair Use Analysis in Santos v. Kimmel
outline.description: This chapter walks through each statutory fair‑use factor under 17 U.S.C. §107 as applied by the district court—and affirmed by the Second Circuit—showing how transformation, nature, amount used, and market effect led to dismissal.
subtopics: "Purpose and character" factor – transformative use doctrine; reasonable observer test versus subjective intent
"Nature" factor – published works created specifically for Cameo requests
"Amount and substantiality" factor – whole videos used but within context of parody/criticism
"Effect on market" factor – no substitute market; reference to Campbell v. Acuff‑Rose on parody exemption
Rejection of plaintiff’s bad‑faith argument citing Harper & Row and subsequent jurisprudence
Court’s reliance on precedent emphasizing flexibility in fair‑use analysis (e.g., Andy Warhol Found., Hachette Book Group)
Affirmation that fair use bars infringement claims at pleading stage when factors are clearly weighted

outline.chapter_title: State Law Contract Claims: Third‑Party Beneficiary Doctrine, Preemption, and Pleading Deficiencies
outline.description: This chapter examines why Santos’s breach‑of‑contract and implied‑contract theories failed—covering third‑party beneficiary presumptions under Illinois law, New York contract formation requirements, preemption by the Copyright Act, and specific pleading shortcomings.
subtopics: Cameo Terms of Service as the alleged contractual basis
Illinois presumption against conferring rights on noncontracting parties; need for express third‑party beneficiary language (Barry v. St. Mary’s Hosp.)
"Express declaration" test vs implied‐in‐fact contract analysis under New York law (Rocky Point Props.; DG & A Mgmt.)
"Essential terms" requirement—failure to allege specific contractual provisions or meeting-of-minds (Caniglia)
Copyright Act preemption doctrine—when state‐law claims are barred because they regulate rights reserved for copyright owners (Melendez v. Sirius XM)
Court’s conclusion that even without preemption analysis plaintiffs failed to state a viable contract claim

outline.\u200bchapter_title\u200b: ​Fraudulent Inducement Claim, Final Holding, and Broader Implications​
outline.\u200bdescription\u200b: ​This final chapter details the elements required for a fraudulent‐inducement action under New York law, explains why Santos’s complaint was deficient for lack of alleged out‑of‑pocket loss, summarizes the Second Circuit’s affirmation order, and discusses the decision’s impact on future fair‑use pleadings and platform contract litigation.​
\u200bsubtopics\u200b: "Fraudulent inducement" elements: misrepresentation, reliance, causation, actual monetary loss (Lama Holding Co.; Connaughton)
"Out‑of‑pocket loss" requirement—Santos’s failure to allege concrete damages
"Affirmation" rationale—district court’s dismissal upheld de novo
Implications for pleading standards in copyright cases—fair use can be securely relied upon at early stages when four factors are clearly weighted
Effect on third‑party rights in online service agreements—reinforcement of strict third‑party beneficiary analysis
